senses.gloss: Dirty, shabby and unpleasant.
examples: We stayed in a *grungy* motel off the highway.
His old sneakers were torn and *grungy*.
That was the *grungiest* apartment I've ever seen.

contrast: Also the plain participle of *guard*: *a heavily guarded building* is protected by guards, not cautious.

senses.gloss: Careful not to show your feelings or give away information.
examples: She gave a *guarded* answer about her plans.
He was polite but *guarded* with reporters.
The senator was more *guarded* in his comments this time.

senses.gloss: Of a medical outlook: uncertain, not clearly hopeful.
examples: Doctors describe his condition as *guarded*.
The prognosis remains *guarded* for now.

contrast: Always a capital *G*, unlike Russian *гватемальский*. It is also a noun: *a Guatemalan*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Guatemala, its people or its culture.
examples: We ate at a small *Guatemalan* restaurant in LA.
Her parents are *Guatemalan*.
The shop sells *Guatemalan* coffee and textiles.

contrast: The adjective for *governor* in American politics, mostly in the news: *a gubernatorial race*. It looks nothing like *governor*, but it shares its Latin root with Russian *губернатор*.

senses.gloss: Relating to a governor or the office of governor.
examples: She's running in the *gubernatorial* election next fall.
The two *gubernatorial* candidates debated on TV.
He lost his *gubernatorial* bid by a few thousand votes.

senses.gloss: Led by a guide or an instructor.
examples: We took a *guided* tour of the Capitol.
The app has *guided* meditations for beginners.
The park offers *guided* hikes every Saturday.

senses.gloss: Steered toward a target by a system inside it.
examples: The navy tested a new *guided* missile.
The plane dropped *laser-guided* bombs.

senses.gloss: Showing the way or directing what someone does.
examples: Honesty has always been our *guiding* principle.
His grandmother was a *guiding* light in his life.
The coach was the *guiding* force behind the team's success.

senses.gloss: Feeling very guilty.
examples: She was *guilt-ridden* after missing her son's game.
He sent me a long, *guilt-ridden* apology.
After the accident, he felt more *guilt-ridden* than ever.

contrast: Russian *доверчивый* can be neutral or even kind; *gullible* always suggests being foolish. For the kind meaning, say *trusting*.

senses.gloss: Easily tricked because you believe what people tell you.
examples: Scammers target *gullible* people online.
Don't be so *gullible* — that story is obviously fake.
My little brother is the most *gullible* person I know.

contrast: In *gummy bears* and *gummy vitamins*, *gummy* comes from the noun *a gummy*, a chewy candy, not from these senses.

senses.gloss: Soft and sticky, like gum.
examples: The rice came out *gummy* because I stirred it too much.
The label left a *gummy* residue on the jar.
This bread is *gummier* than it should be.

senses.gloss: Showing a lot of gum, or having no teeth.
examples: The baby gave us a big *gummy* smile.
She used to be embarrassed by her *gummy* smile.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *a gung-ho attitude*
form: from a Chinese phrase meaning *work together*, used as a US Marine slogan

senses.gloss: Very enthusiastic and eager, sometimes too eager.
examples: The new manager is really *gung ho* about teamwork.
He had a *gung-ho* attitude that annoyed some of the older staff.
She was more *gung ho* about the camping trip than any of us.

position: both — sense 2 only before a noun

senses.gloss: Praising someone or something with too much emotion.
examples: The movie got *gushing* reviews from critics.
She wrote a *gushing* post about her new boss.
His introduction was even more *gushing* than last year's.

senses.gloss: Flowing out fast and in large amounts.
examples: *Gushing* water flooded the basement.
It took crews three days to cap the *gushing* well.

senses.gloss: With the wind blowing in sudden strong bursts.
examples: Expect *gusty* winds this afternoon.
It was cold and *gusty* at the beach.
Tomorrow will be even *gustier*, so tie down the patio chairs.

senses.gloss: Lacking courage or determination.
examples: It was a *gutless* decision to cancel the vote.
Critics called the mayor *gutless*.
I've never seen a more *gutless* performance from this team.

senses.gloss: Brave and willing to take risks.
examples: That was a *gutsy* call on fourth down.
She's *gutsy* — she quit her job to start a business.
It was the *gutsiest* move of his career.

senses.gloss: Made deep in the throat and sounding rough.
examples: The dog let out a low, *guttural* growl.
Some languages sound *guttural* to English speakers.
His laugh was deeper and more *guttural* than I expected.

contrast: American spelling *gynecological*; British English writes *gynaecological*. The *g* is hard, as in *guy*.

senses.gloss: Relating to women's reproductive health and its medical care.
examples: She has a *gynecological* exam once a year.
The clinic treats a range of *gynecological* conditions.
He specializes in *gynecological* surgery.

senses.gloss: Causing a habit or addiction that is hard to stop.
examples: Some sleeping pills can be *habit-forming*.
Many apps are designed to be *habit-forming*.
Nicotine is more *habit-forming* than most people realize.

contrast: *Inhabitable* means the same as *habitable*, not the opposite. The opposite is *uninhabitable*.

senses.gloss: Good enough for people to live in.
examples: The cabin needs a lot of work before it's *habitable*.
Astronomers are searching for *habitable* planets.
After the repairs, the house was far more *habitable*.

position: both — sense 2 only before a noun

senses.gloss: Done regularly, as a habit.
examples: He greeted us with his *habitual* smile.
Her lateness had become *habitual*.
Over the years, his drinking became more *habitual*.

senses.gloss: Doing something bad again and again.
examples: He's a *habitual* liar.
The new law targets *habitual* offenders.

senses.gloss: Used so often that it has lost its effect.
examples: The speech was full of *hackneyed* phrases.
The plot felt *hackneyed* and predictable.
It's hard to think of a more *hackneyed* ending than 'it was all a dream.'

senses.gloss: Looking very tired, worried or ill.
examples: After three night shifts, she looked pale and *haggard*.
A *haggard* man was waiting at the door.
He looked even more *haggard* after the trial.

form: compound — noun + participle: it makes your hair stand up

senses.gloss: Very frightening or dangerous, often in an exciting way.
senses.ru: жуткий, от которого волосы встают дыбом
examples: We had a *hair-raising* drive down the mountain in the snow.
The landing was pretty *hair-raising*.
Her stories from the war zone were even more *hair-raising*.

senses.gloss: Having no hair.
examples: Sphynx cats are almost completely *hairless*.
Newborn mice are pink and *hairless*.
He rubbed his *hairless* head and laughed.

senses.gloss: Covered with a lot of hair.
examples: He has big *hairy* arms.
Our dog gets really *hairy* in the winter.
My dad is *hairier* than anyone else in the family.

senses.gloss: Informal: frightening or risky.
examples: Things got a little *hairy* when the boat started leaking.
That was a *hairy* moment on the freeway.

contrast: Always a capital *H*. It is also a noun: *a Haitian*. The language is *Haitian Creole*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Haiti, its people or its culture.
examples: Miami has a large *Haitian* community.
My neighbor is *Haitian*.
We tried *Haitian* food for the first time last week.

senses.gloss: Prepared or allowed according to Islamic law.
examples: The cafeteria now offers *halal* meals.
Is this chicken *halal*?
There's a *halal* butcher shop on our street.

contrast: Almost always in *halcyon days*: a happy, peaceful time in the past, remembered with nostalgia.

senses.gloss: Happy and peaceful, usually about a time in the past.
examples: He often talks about the *halcyon* days of his college years.
Those were the *halcyon* days of the company, before the layoffs.
She wrote about one *halcyon* summer at the lake.

contrast: Most uses of *half* are not this adjective: in *half an hour* and *half the class* it stands before *a* or *the* (a predeterminer), in *cut it in half* it is a noun, and in *half empty* it is an adverb. American English says both *half an hour* and *a half hour*.

senses.gloss: Being one of two equal parts of something.
examples: Can I get a *half* order of fries?
We only have a *half* day of school on Friday.
He owns a *half* share in the restaurant.

senses.gloss: Partial, not complete.
examples: *Half* measures won't fix this problem.
She gave me a *half* smile and looked away.

form: compound — adverb + participle: not fully baked

senses.gloss: Not properly thought out or planned.
examples: He came up with another *half-baked* plan to get rich.
The idea sounds *half-baked* to me.
Honestly, this proposal is even more *half-baked* than the last one.

contrast: Also spelled *halfhearted*, the main spelling in American dictionaries; both are common.

senses.gloss: Done without real effort, interest or enthusiasm.
examples: He made a *half-hearted* attempt to clean his room.
Her apology sounded *half-hearted*.
The applause was even more *half-hearted* after the second speech.

contrast: Also spelled *half-hearted*; the meaning is the same.

senses.gloss: Showing little effort or enthusiasm.
examples: The team gave a *halfhearted* effort in the second half.
She was *halfhearted* about the move from the start.
I've rarely seen a more *halfhearted* campaign.

contrast: Most often an adverb: *We're halfway there*; *Meet me halfway*. Only before a noun is it this adjective.

senses.gloss: In the middle between two points or between the start and the end.
examples: We stopped for lunch at the *halfway* point.
The team was ahead at the *halfway* mark.
By the *halfway* stage of the race, she was in third place.

senses.gloss: Partial, not going far enough.
examples: *Halfway* measures won't satisfy voters.
There's no *halfway* solution to this.

senses.gloss: Holy; made sacred.
examples: The battlefield is *hallowed* ground.
The old church stands on *hallowed* soil.

senses.gloss: Greatly respected because of long tradition.
examples: He finally walked the *hallowed* halls of Harvard.
Fenway Park is one of baseball's most *hallowed* places.
Many Americans treat the Constitution as a *hallowed* document.

senses.gloss: Causing you to see or hear things that are not really there.
examples: Some wild mushrooms are *hallucinogenic*.
The study tested a *hallucinogenic* drug as a treatment for depression.
Police found *hallucinogenic* substances in the car.

senses.gloss: Slow and stopping often, because of doubt or difficulty.
examples: He apologized in *halting* English.
Her voice was quiet and *halting*.
The recovery has been slower and more *halting* than expected.

form: compound — *ham* + *fist* + -ed: hands as big and clumsy as hams
contrast: *Ham-handed* means the same and is the more American of the two.

senses.gloss: Clumsy, with the hands or in dealing with people.
examples: It was a *ham-fisted* attempt at humor.
I'm too *ham-fisted* to repair watches.
The company's response was even more *ham-fisted* than the original mistake.

contrast: Same meaning as *ham-fisted*.

senses.gloss: Clumsy or tactless.
examples: The mayor's *ham-handed* handling of the strike made things worse.
He's a little *ham-handed* in the kitchen.
Their marketing was more *ham-handed* than clever.

position: both — sense 1 mostly after a verb
contrast: *The team got hammered* is usually the passive verb: they were badly beaten.

senses.gloss: Slang: very drunk.
examples: He got *hammered* at the bachelor party.
By midnight, half the guests were completely *hammered*.
I can't drive — I'm *hammered*.

senses.gloss: Shaped or marked by hitting with a hammer.
examples: She wore a *hammered* silver bracelet.
The farmhouse sink is made of *hammered* copper.

contrast: Nothing to do with meat: *a ham* here is an actor who overacts.

senses.gloss: Acting in an exaggerated, overly dramatic way.
examples: The villain's *hammy* performance made the audience laugh.
His acting was a little *hammy*.
The sequel is even *hammier* than the original.

contrast: Often spelled as one word, *handcrafted*. Close to *handmade*, but *hand-crafted* stresses skill and care.

senses.gloss: Made by hand with skill.
examples: The shop sells *hand-crafted* furniture.
Every piece of jewelry is *hand-crafted*.
We bought a *hand-crafted* cutting board at the county fair.

contrast: Also a noun: *I wore my sister's hand-me-downs*.

senses.gloss: Used first by someone else, usually an older brother or sister, and then passed on to you.
examples: I grew up wearing *hand-me-down* clothes.
He learned to play on a *hand-me-down* guitar.
Our first car was a *hand-me-down* minivan from my parents.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb, written without hyphens: *They fought hand to hand*.

senses.gloss: Of fighting: at very close range, with the hands or hand weapons.
examples: Soldiers are trained in *hand-to-hand* combat.
The movie ends with a *hand-to-hand* fight on a rooftop.
It was brutal *hand-to-hand* fighting in the streets.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb, written without hyphens: *They lived hand to mouth*.

senses.gloss: Having only just enough money to live on, with nothing saved.
examples: They lived a *hand-to-mouth* existence for years.
Many gig workers have a *hand-to-mouth* lifestyle.
He grew up in a *hand-to-mouth* family in rural Ohio.

contrast: Also a noun: *a handheld* is a small device, such as a game console.

senses.gloss: Small enough to hold and use in your hand.
examples: The kids played *handheld* video games in the car.
He shot the whole film with a *handheld* camera.
The scanner is light and fully *handheld*.

contrast: Now considered dated and often offensive about people; say *disabled* or *a person with a disability*. It survives on signs and in set phrases: *handicapped parking*, *handicapped-accessible*.

senses.gloss: Having a physical or mental disability.
examples: Park in the *handicapped* spaces only if you have a permit.
The bathroom on the first floor is *handicapped-accessible*.
The program was set up in the 1970s for *handicapped* children.

senses.gloss: Made by hand, not by machine.
examples: She gave me a *handmade* birthday card.
All their soaps are *handmade*.
The market is full of *handmade* pottery.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb, usually without a hyphen: *She won hands down*; *It's hands down the best pizza in town*.

senses.gloss: Clear and easy, with no doubt at all.
examples: She was the *hands-down* winner.
This movie is the *hands-down* favorite for best picture.
It was a *hands-down* victory for the home team.

senses.gloss: Letting people do things their own way, without getting involved.
examples: My boss has a *hands-off* management style.
The government took a *hands-off* approach to the industry.
My parents were more *hands-off* with my younger brother.

senses.gloss: Involving doing things yourself, not just reading or watching.
examples: The museum has lots of *hands-on* exhibits for kids.
Nothing beats *hands-on* experience.
The course is very *hands-on*.

senses.gloss: Personally involved in the work and its details.
examples: She's a *hands-on* manager who knows every client.
My dad was more *hands-on* with us than his father ever was.

position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
contrast: About a man, *handsome* is the usual word for good-looking; *pretty* and *beautiful* are mostly for women. About a woman, *handsome* means striking and strong-featured, not delicate. The *d* is silent.

senses.gloss: Good-looking, especially of a man.
examples: Her husband is tall and *handsome*.
He was the *handsomest* guy in our class.
What a *handsome* little boy!

senses.gloss: Of a thing or an animal: attractive and well made.
examples: They live in a *handsome* brick house on Elm Street.
That's a *handsome* leather jacket.

senses.gloss: Of money: large in amount.
examples: She sold the company for a *handsome* profit.
They offered a *handsome* reward for the lost dog.

senses.gloss: Written by hand with a pen or pencil.
examples: She left a *handwritten* note on the door.
The recipe is *handwritten* on an old index card.
A *handwritten* thank-you letter means a lot.

position: both — sense 2 only after a verb or a noun
contrast: *Come in handy* means turn out to be useful: *This flashlight will come in handy*.

senses.gloss: Useful and easy to use.
examples: This app is really *handy* for splitting the bill.
Keep the receipt — it might come in *handy*.
The new version is even *handier* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Near and easy to reach.
examples: Do you have a pen *handy*?
Keep a flashlight *handy* in case the power goes out.

senses.gloss: Good at fixing or making things with your hands.
examples: My husband is *handy* with tools.
It helps to be *handy* if you buy an old house.

senses.gloss: Done without any plan or order.
examples: Books were stacked in a *haphazard* way on the floor.
Their approach to safety was pretty *haphazard*.
The second half of the project was even more *haphazard* than the first.

senses.gloss: Unlucky, often in a way that looks a little foolish.
examples: The *hapless* tourists got lost again.
The team's *hapless* defense gave up six goals.
The *hapless* intern spilled coffee on the CEO.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and not worried about the future.
examples: He was a *happy-go-lucky* kid who made friends everywhere.
She seems *happy-go-lucky*, but she works incredibly hard.
My younger brother was always more *happy-go-lucky* than me.

contrast: The adjective describes someone stressed by too many demands (*a harassed waiter*). *She was harassed at work* is the passive verb: someone treated her in a hostile or sexual way, a much more serious meaning. Some Americans stress the first syllable: HAIR-uhst.

senses.gloss: Tired, anxious and stressed because of too many problems or demands.
examples: A *harassed* mom was trying to calm three kids at the checkout.
The waiter looked *harassed* and overworked.
By Friday, the staff looked more *harassed* than ever.

position: predicative only — never before a noun

senses.gloss: Not having enough money, or not enough of something you need.
examples: We were pretty *hard up* when I was a kid.
The school is *hard up* for volunteers this year.
After the plant closed, the town was more *hard up* than ever.

contrast: Usually in the negative: *There are no hard-and-fast rules*.

senses.gloss: Fixed and not able to be changed.
examples: There are no *hard-and-fast* rules for raising kids.
We don't have a *hard-and-fast* deadline yet.
It's more of a guideline than a *hard-and-fast* rule.

senses.gloss: Tough and not easily shocked, because of hard experience.
examples: The story is told by a *hard-bitten* detective.
Even *hard-bitten* reporters were shocked by the photos.
The old sailors were more *hard-bitten* than anyone else on the crew.

comparison: not gradable — sense 2 can take *more*: *more hard-boiled*

senses.gloss: Of an egg: boiled until the yolk is solid.
examples: I packed two *hard-boiled* eggs for lunch.
Do you want your eggs *hard-boiled* or soft?

senses.gloss: Tough and unemotional, especially in crime fiction.
examples: He loves old *hard-boiled* detective novels.
She plays a *hard-boiled* cop in the new series.

senses.gloss: Won or achieved only with great effort against strong opposition.
examples: It was a *hard-fought* victory over a tough team.
Workers won *hard-fought* gains in the new contract.
The game was close and *hard-fought* from start to finish.

senses.gloss: Direct and forceful in dealing with a serious problem.
examples: The newspaper published a *hard-hitting* report on police misconduct.
Her documentary is *hard-hitting* and honest.
This year's anti-smoking ads are more *hard-hitting* than last year's.

senses.gloss: In sports: hitting or tackling with a lot of force.
examples: He's a big, *hard-hitting* linebacker.
It was a *hard-hitting* game with lots of injuries.

contrast: Also written *hardline*. A person with these views is *a hard-liner*.

senses.gloss: Refusing to change your views or compromise, especially in politics.
examples: The governor took a *hard-line* position on crime.
*Hard-line* members of the party blocked the deal.
His views have become more *hard-line* over the years.

senses.gloss: Tough, practical and not influenced by feelings.
examples: She's a *hard-nosed* negotiator.
He takes a *hard-nosed* approach to business.
The new coach is more *hard-nosed* than the last one.

contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (*hard-of-hearing students*); after a verb it is usually three separate words: *My grandpa is hard of hearing*. *Deaf* means unable to hear at all.

senses.gloss: Not able to hear well, but not completely deaf.
examples: The theater offers headsets for *hard-of-hearing* guests.
My grandpa is a little *hard of hearing*, so speak up.
The school has services for deaf and *hard-of-hearing* students.

position: both — sense 1 only after a verb

senses.gloss: Having great difficulty doing something.
examples: You'd be *hard-pressed* to find a better deal.
I'm *hard-pressed* to remember the last time it snowed here.

senses.gloss: Under a lot of pressure, especially from lack of money or time.
examples: *Hard-pressed* families are struggling with rising rents.
Hospitals were more *hard-pressed* than ever that winter.
The *hard-pressed* staff worked double shifts.

contrast: Also written *hard-core*. In *hardcore pornography* it means sexually explicit; *hardcore punk* is a style of music.

senses.gloss: Very committed and enthusiastic, more than most people.
examples: Only the *hardcore* fans stayed in the rain.
She's a *hardcore* gamer.
My brother is way more *hardcore* about fitness than I am.

senses.gloss: Extreme or very intense.
examples: That was a *hardcore* workout.
Camping in January is pretty *hardcore*.

contrast: Also a noun: *The book came out in hardcover*. British English prefers *hardback*.

senses.gloss: Of a book: with a stiff, strong cover.
examples: The *hardcover* edition costs thirty dollars.
I bought a *hardcover* copy for my dad.
The library replaced its worn *hardcover* books with paperbacks.

senses.gloss: Made tough by experience, so no longer shocked or upset.
examples: He's a *hardened* criminal with a long record.
After years at war, she had become *hardened* to violence.
He came back from prison more *hardened* than before.

senses.gloss: Made physically hard or firm.
examples: The blade is made of *hardened* steel.
Scrape off the *hardened* glue before you paint.

senses.gloss: Practical and realistic, not emotional.
examples: We need to take a *hardheaded* look at the budget.
She's a *hardheaded* businesswoman.

senses.gloss: Stubborn and unwilling to listen.
examples: My dad is too *hardheaded* to ask for directions.
Why are you being so *hardheaded*?
He's even more *hardheaded* than his mother.

contrast: Also written *hard-line*; the meaning is the same.

senses.gloss: Strict and unwilling to compromise, especially in politics.
examples: The party's *hardline* wing opposed any compromise.
Critics say the new policy is too *hardline*.
The talks collapsed after both sides grew more *hardline*.

form: compound — *hard* + *scrabble*, to scratch around for something

senses.gloss: Poor, and needing very hard work to make a living.
examples: He grew up on a *hardscrabble* farm in West Texas.
Her memoir describes a *hardscrabble* childhood in Appalachia.
It was a *hardscrabble* mining town with one diner and two bars.

contrast: Do not confuse with *hearty* (warm and friendly; large, as in *a hearty meal*), which sounds similar.

senses.gloss: Strong and able to live through difficult conditions.
examples: Only a few *hardy* hikers made it to the top.
Goats are *hardy* animals.
The *hardiest* fans showed up in the snow.

senses.gloss: Of a plant: able to survive cold weather outdoors.
examples: These roses are *hardy* enough for Minnesota winters.
Kale is *hardier* than lettuce.

form: compound — *hare* + *brain* + -ed: with a brain like a rabbit's
contrast: Spelled with *hare* (a kind of rabbit), not *hair*.

senses.gloss: Foolish and not likely to work.
examples: He's always coming up with *harebrained* schemes.
That idea is completely *harebrained*.
Her latest plan is even more *harebrained* than the last.

senses.gloss: Causing damage or injury.
examples: Too much sun is *harmful* to your skin.
The factory released *harmful* chemicals into the river.
Some doctors think sugar is more *harmful* than fat.

senses.gloss: Not able to cause damage or injury.
examples: Most spiders are *harmless* to people.
The substance is completely *harmless*.
Garter snakes look scary, but they're *harmless*.

senses.gloss: Not meant to hurt or offend anyone.
examples: It was just *harmless* fun.
He's a little annoying, but *harmless*.

senses.gloss: Friendly and peaceful, without disagreement.
examples: They have a *harmonious* relationship with their neighbors.
The office has become much more *harmonious* since the reorganization.
Life at home was not always *harmonious*.

senses.gloss: Of colors, sounds or parts: fitting together in a pleasant way.
examples: The room has a *harmonious* mix of colors.
The choir's voices were beautifully *harmonious*.

contrast: Close to *harassed* in its adjective sense, and more common in American English. Nothing to do with the name *Harry*.

senses.gloss: Stressed and rushed because of too many demands.
examples: A *harried* waitress finally took our order.
Parents look *harried* during the holiday rush.
The nurses were more *harried* than usual on Monday.

senses.gloss: Extremely frightening or upsetting to live through.
examples: The survivors described a *harrowing* night in the lifeboat.
The documentary is *harrowing* but important.
It was the most *harrowing* experience of my life.

senses.gloss: Unkind, cruel or too severe.
examples: The judge handed down a *harsh* sentence.
Don't be so *harsh* on yourself.
Her *harshest* critics were her own teammates.

senses.gloss: Of conditions or weather: very difficult to live in.
examples: These plants survive *harsh* desert conditions.
Winters in North Dakota are *harsh*.
The climate was *harsher* than they had expected.

senses.gloss: Too strong or unpleasant for the eyes, ears or skin.
examples: The *harsh* office lights gave me a headache.
This soap is too *harsh* for a baby's skin.

contrast: Always a capital *H*. Also spelled *Chasidic*, and some speakers begin it with the throaty sound of German *Bach*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to a strictly Orthodox Jewish movement.
examples: Brooklyn has a large *Hasidic* community.
Their neighbors are *Hasidic*.
*Hasidic* men often wear black coats and hats.

senses.gloss: Done too quickly, without enough thought.
examples: Let's not make any *hasty* decisions.
Maybe I was too *hasty* in judging him.
Looking back, the decision seems *hasty*.

senses.gloss: Done or made very quickly because there is little time.
examples: We ate a *hasty* breakfast and ran for the bus.
The robbers made a *hasty* exit.
The second draft was even *hastier* than the first.

contrast: Not *hateful*: a *hated* person is hated by others; a *hateful* person is full of hate.

senses.gloss: Strongly disliked by many people.
examples: He was the most *hated* man in town.
The new parking rules are widely *hated*.
Traffic cameras are a *hated* part of city life.

contrast: *Hateful* usually means full of hate (*hateful comments*), not *hated* by others.

senses.gloss: Full of hate, or very cruel toward others.
examples: He posted *hateful* comments online.
What a *hateful* thing to say!
Her words were more *hateful* than anything I'd heard before.

senses.gloss: Behaving as if you are better than other people.
examples: The *haughty* waiter ignored our table.
She gave me a cold, *haughty* look.
He's become even *haughtier* since his promotion.

senses.gloss: Believed to be visited by ghosts.
examples: Kids say the old house on the hill is *haunted*.
We went through a *haunted* house at Halloween.
It's supposedly the most *haunted* hotel in America.

senses.gloss: Troubled for a long time by a memory or a worry.
examples: He had a *haunted* look in his eyes.
She is still *haunted* by the accident.

contrast: Not *haunted*: a *haunting* song stays in your mind; a *haunted* house has ghosts.

senses.gloss: Beautiful, sad or frightening in a way that stays in your mind.
examples: The song has a *haunting* melody.
Her photographs of the war are *haunting*.
It's one of the most *haunting* movies I've ever seen.

contrast: Always a capital *H*. As a noun, *a Hawaiian* strictly means a Native Hawaiian; someone who simply lives there is *a Hawaii resident*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Hawaii, its people, language or culture.
examples: He wore a *Hawaiian* shirt to the barbecue.
*Hawaiian* pizza has ham and pineapple on it.
She's taking a class in the *Hawaiian* language.

senses.gloss: Able to notice small details; watching very closely.
examples: A *hawk-eyed* fan spotted the mistake in the credits.
The teacher is *hawk-eyed* during exams.
Our editor is even more *hawk-eyed* than the proofreader.

senses.gloss: Favoring military force or tough action in foreign policy.
examples: The senator is known for his *hawkish* views on foreign policy.
His advisers were more *hawkish* than the public.

senses.gloss: In economics: favoring higher interest rates to fight inflation.
examples: The Fed's *hawkish* tone worried investors.
Stocks fell after *hawkish* comments from the central bank.

position: predicative only — almost always after *go*: *go haywire*
form: *hay* + *wire*: the wire used to tie hay bales, which tangled easily

senses.gloss: Not working properly, or out of control.
examples: My phone went *haywire* after the update.
The thermostat has gone *haywire* again.
Everything went *haywire* when the power came back on.

senses.gloss: Dangerous, especially to health or safety.
examples: The plant disposes of *hazardous* waste.
Smoking is *hazardous* to your health.
Driving is more *hazardous* in winter.

contrast: Mostly about eyes: a light brown mixed with green or gold, lighter than a typical Russian *карий*. Plain dark brown eyes are just *brown*. As a noun, *hazel* is also the tree that gives hazelnuts.

senses.gloss: Light brown with some green or gold, especially of eyes.
examples: She has big *hazel* eyes.
His eyes are *hazel*, not green.
The baby's eyes turned *hazel* by her first birthday.

senses.gloss: Of air or sky: not clear because of mist, smoke or dust.
examples: It was a hot, *hazy* afternoon.
The mountains looked *hazy* in the distance.
The sky is *hazier* than usual because of the wildfires.

senses.gloss: Not clear in your mind; vague.
examples: My memory of that night is a little *hazy*.
I'm still *hazy* on the details of the plan.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb: *The cars collided head-on*; *We need to face the problem head-on*.

senses.gloss: With the fronts of two things hitting each other.
examples: Two people were hurt in a *head-on* collision on Route 9.
It was a *head-on* crash at highway speed.

senses.gloss: Direct, without avoiding a problem or a conflict.
examples: The mayor took a *head-on* approach to the housing crisis.
The two sides are headed for a *head-on* clash over taxes.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb, often without hyphens: *The two stores compete head to head*.

senses.gloss: Involving direct competition between two people or teams.
examples: The two candidates will meet in a *head-to-head* debate.
It's a *head-to-head* battle for first place.
In *head-to-head* matchups, Boston has won six of the last ten.

senses.gloss: Without a head.
examples: The story is about a *headless* horseman.
We found a *headless* doll in the attic.
The statue has stood *headless* since the earthquake.

contrast: More often an adverb: *She rushed headlong into marriage*; *He fell headlong down the stairs*.

senses.gloss: With the head first.
examples: He made a *headlong* dive into the pool.
She took a *headlong* fall down the stairs.

senses.gloss: Very fast and without careful thought.
examples: The *headlong* rush into new technology worries some teachers.
It was a *headlong* flight from the burning building.

senses.gloss: Determined to do things your own way, without listening to advice.
examples: She was a *headstrong* teenager.
He's too *headstrong* to take anyone's advice.
Their second child is even more *headstrong* than the first.

senses.gloss: So exciting that it makes you feel a little out of control.
examples: Those were the *heady* days of the dot-com boom.
Winning the title was a *heady* experience for such a young team.
It was the *headiest* moment of her career.

senses.gloss: Of a drink or a smell: strong, making you feel a little drunk or dizzy.
examples: It's a *heady* red wine.
The *heady* scent of jasmine filled the garden.
